newsitem.title: USA: Rap music label Death Row faces probe.
newsitem.headline: Rap music label Death Row faces probe.

text.p: With its founder in jail, its major star murdered and its bookkeeper in hiding, the tangled past of the record label that helped pioneer Gangsta Rap music is quickly catching up with it.

Since the murder last year of star Tupac Shakur, Death Row records has faced problems ranging from lawsuits to a federal probe on whether it was started with drug money. There is also an investigation to find out why one prosecutor's daughter got a $50,000 recording contract with the label.

Death Row would not comment on the probe or litigation. But legal sources said a grand jury has convened in Los Angeles after a long investigation into the label -- which delivered a string of multi-platimum Gangsta hits in its heyday.
The grand jury will hear allegations of racketeering, links to street gangs, violent crime, drug trafficking and money laundering against the label, the sources said.
The black-owned label suffered another blow in February when its owner, Marion "Suge" Knight, was sentenced to 9 years for violating his parole on assault charges.

Federal officials in Los Angeles have been focusing on the relationship between Knight, his lawyer David Kenner and convicted drug dealer Michael "Harry-O" Harris, according to sources close to the investigation.
Harris, Knight and Kenner, who is reportedly recovering from heart surgery, were unavailable for comment.

"Harris has said he was cheated out of money. That is what I and others have heard him saying for years and based on what I know, there is no reason to disbelieve him," said an associate of Harris familiar with the investigation.

Sources said Harris, serving a 28-year sentence, claims he put up $1.5 million while behind bars in 1991 to launch Death Row during a visit from Knight and Kenner and was then cheated out of millions of dollars in profits.
Harris was moved from a state prison to Los Angeles, fanning speculation he will testify before the grand jury.
Questions about its financial dealings have dogged the label since its start and they intensified after Shakur was shot in Las Vegas while in a car with Knight.
"The label's future is obviously dubious with Knight out of commission," said one executive at a major label.
Greg Howard, a Death Row spokesman, said the label was still producing records and is being run by Knight's brother-in-law, Norris Anderson.
Death Row racked up an estimated $300 million in sales but never turned a profit due to high debts and Knight's extravagant spending habits, lawyers and other sources said.

Shakur's mother, Afeni Shakur, a former Black Panther activist, has gone after the label since learning her son died $4.9 million dollars in debt, despite having sold more than than $60 million worth of records.
"We believe Death Row withheld royalty payments from Tupac and failed to deliver advances promised under his contract," Shakur's lawyer Richard Fischbein said.
Shakur's mother filed a lawsuit in April against Death Row, Knight and Kenner, seeking $150 million in damages. She said the two sides are currently in negotiations.
Then, there is the case of the missing accountant.

Coopers & Lybrand, Death Row's former auditors, have turned over all records handled by bookkeeper Steve Cantrock. The firm declined to comment on Cantrock's whereabouts but sources said he went into hiding after threats were made to his life.

Also, the California State Attorney General's office is investigating Los Angeles Deputy District Attorney Lawrence Longo, who oversaw Knight's probation and was discharged March 31 for conflict of interest. Among the allegations against Longo are that his teenage daughter signed a $50,000 record deal with Death Row and that Longo leased his home to Kenner, Knight's attorney.

"Longo was the prosecutor in Suge Knight's case and the evidence shows that Longo's family trust rented his Malibu home to David Kenner -- the defence attorney for Knight -- and that he knew Marion Knight was going to be the primary occupant of the beach house," said Steve Sowders, a spokesman for the L.A. District Attorney's office.
"Therein lies the conflict. He was prosecuting him while he had him as a tenant for $20,000 a month," Sowders said.
Hearings for Longo's reinstatement have been scheduled for August and September. Among the witnesses being subpoenaed are Knight's attorney, Kenner, a central link to Death Row's saga.
